## Findings

- **Overall parity within statistical noise:** Across the 30 benchmark questions (90 evaluation runs pooled over 3 repeats), all three architectures achieved comparable overall correctness rates (Dense RAG: 70% [52%, 83%], Hybrid RAG: 67% [49%, 81%], GraphRAG: 70% [52%, 83%]). Because the 95% Wilson confidence intervals overlap substantially, no architecture demonstrated a statistically distinguishable aggregate advantage at this sample size.
- **Where GraphRAG succeeded (Relational discovery and hallucination bounding):** GraphRAG tied for the highest correctness pass rate on relational questions (75% [41%, 93%], outperforming Hybrid at 50%) by exploiting explicit inter-page doc links and code symbol references. Crucially, GraphRAG achieved the highest correct abstention on unanswerable queries (67% [21%, 94%] compared to 33% for Dense and Hybrid); when concepts do not connect in the graph, candidate expansion naturally terminates, avoiding retrieving deceptive distractor chunks that induce hallucinations.
- **Where GraphRAG lost (Exact identifiers and Multi-hop complexity):** GraphRAG lagged on exact reference questions (75% [30%, 95%] vs 100% for Dense and Hybrid; page retrieval hit dropped to 0.75 and MRR to 0.46) and multi-hop queries (62% vs 75%). For specific error codes, configuration parameters, and named methods, lexical BM25 and dense similarity pinpoint the target chunk immediately, whereas 2-hop BFS expansion through high-degree hub nodes introduced peripheral noise into the context window.
- **The cost-benefit imbalance:** Hybrid RAG delivered the strongest overall page retrieval performance (1.00 hit@8, 0.92 recall@8, 0.93 MRR) at negligible indexing cost. In contrast, GraphRAG required 751 extraction calls (629k tokens, 68 minutes of LLM inference) and produced 13/30 false merges in embedding-based entity resolution (clustering opposites like "before" vs "after"). Dense index construction completed in under 3 minutes with zero LLM API dependency.
- **Bottom line:** Hybrid RAG (BM25 + Dense with RRF) provides the optimal trade-off of engineering simplicity, low latency, and retrieval accuracy for technical manuals. A graph layer is justified primarily when domain requirements prioritize relational traceability or strict abstention on ungrounded concepts.

## Limits

- **Corpus scale:** The evaluation is conducted on a pinned subset of 47 LangGraph documentation pages (732 chunks, ~179k tokens). Large-scale industrial repositories with hundreds of thousands of cross-linked documents will exhibit different graph density, community structures, and hub saturation dynamics.
- **Benchmark sample size:** While 30 carefully curated questions across 5 distinct categories provide meaningful directional signal, the per-category sample size (n=3 to 8) results in wide 95% Wilson intervals (spanning 30-40 percentage points). Distinguishing fine architectural nuances would require 100+ questions.
- **Single-model evaluation family:** A single LLM family (`nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning-30b-a3b`) was used for extraction, answering, and automated judging. Although judge prompts enforced atomic claim verification and abstentions were evaluated deterministically, residual model evaluation bias cannot be entirely ruled out without full manual ground-truth calibration.
- **Graph expansion tuning:** The graph retriever uses a uniform 2-hop BFS expansion with degree-capping (max hub degree 40) and fallback. While effective, alternative graph traversal algorithms such as personalized PageRank or community summarization could alter GraphRAG performance characteristics.

## What I would do at Safran

- **Ground graphs in physical and engineering hierarchies:** In aerospace maintenance and systems engineering (AMM, IPC, ATA chapters, engine component break-downs), documentation follows physical assemblies. I would build the graph skeleton deterministically from PLM, CAD, and maintenance catalogs rather than relying on noisy unsupervised LLM triplet extraction.
- **Standardize on Hybrid RAG for procedural manuals:** Deploy BM25 (custom-tokenized for part numbers, MIL-STD references, and fault isolation codes) fused with dense embeddings for primary troubleshooting and task-oriented procedural queries, ensuring sub-100ms retrieval without graph extraction cost.
- **Deploy GraphRAG for cross-system fault propagation:** Use graph traversals specifically for cross-system impact analysis (e.g., determining which actuators, flight control channels, and cockpit indications are impacted by an intermittent sensor fault across multiple ATA chapters).
- **Enforce deterministic catalog-based entity resolution:** Aviation compliance cannot tolerate heuristic embedding merges that risk conflating parts or revisions (e.g., Part-101 vs Part-101R). All entity merges should be strictly validated against enterprise master data catalogs.
- **Implement atomic claim traceability for airworthiness:** Embed the atomic claim verification mechanism into the retrieval and generation pipeline, guaranteeing that every maintenance recommendation or torque specification cites verified, version-controlled technical manuals for regulatory compliance.
